title: Contribution
text: We developed PRINCE, a software model designed to address a major challenge in de novo minibinder development: identifying biologically relevant binding regions before initiating resource-intensive protein design campaigns. While tools such as RFdiffusion, BindCraft, and BoltzGen have made computational protein design more accessible, identifying effective binding sites remains a challenge. Minibinders that demonstrate strong computational predictions often fail to achieve comparable results in experimental settings. Successful minibinder design therefore requires not only generating promising candidates but also identifying and targeting suitable epitopes. After our initial Deformed Wing Virus (DWV) minibinder campaign produced no confirmed binding hits, we developed PRINCE to integrate structural analysis with existing experimental literature. The software evaluates solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), hydrophobic residue distributions, and local structural properties while using a large language model (LLM) to extract relevant biological evidence from published research. title: Contribution
text: PRINCE contributes to the synthetic biology community by providing an accessible, open-source approach to literature-informed epitope identification that future iGEM teams can apply to their own protein targets. By integrating structural predictions with published biological evidence, our software reduces the need for researchers to manually evaluate extensive literature and independently identify promising binding regions. We released PRINCE as a web application for teams without a programming background, a command-line interface for teams integrating it into an existing design pipeline, and a GitLab repository holding the source code, documentation, and datasets. Through PRINCE, we aim to lower technical barriers to computational protein engineering and establish a reusable framework that future teams can utilize for applications beyond DWV.

title: Contribution
section: How to Replicate and Use PRINCE
text: Access the software: Open the PRINCE web application or download the source code from Lambert iGEM’s GitLab repository. Prepare a target structure: Obtain the protein’s three-dimensional structure from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) or another suitable structural source. Run structural analysis: Use PRINCE to evaluate solvent accessibility, hydrophobicity, and local structural properties to identify potential binding regions. Incorporate literature: Use PRINCE’s LLM-assisted literature analysis to evaluate published evidence concerning functional regions, binding interactions, and experimentally characterized epitopes. Evaluate ranked hotspots: Review the resulting epitope rankings and supporting evidence to select promising regions for downstream protein design. Design and validate minibinders: Incorporate selected hotspots into compatible design pipelines, such as RFdiffusion or BindCraft, and evaluate candidate binders computationally and experimentally.

title: Contribution
text: We designed a minibinder against green fluorescent protein (GFP) and contributed it to the Registry as a general-purpose reagent for the iGEM community. GFP remains among the most widely used reporters in synthetic biology, and teams working with GFP-tagged constructs frequently need a binding partner for pull-down, immobilization, localization, and detection work. Commercial anti-GFP nanobodies serve this role well but carry costs that place them outside many team budgets, particularly for high school teams and teams in low-resource settings. A freely available, documented binder sequence that a team can order and express directly removes that barrier. We designed this part computationally rather than selecting it experimentally. Candidate epitopes on the GFP surface were ranked using PRINCE, our literature-informed epitope prioritization framework, and minibinders were generated against the highest-ranked sites using the same workflow we applied to our Deformed Wing Virus designs. We have published the design rationale, the selected epitope, and the full pipeline parameters so that teams can evaluate the reasoning behind the sequence rather than accepting it on trust.

title: Contribution
text: Few reagents have the potential to benefit as many iGEM teams as a GFP-binding minibinder. For over two decades, green fluorescent protein (GFP) has been widely used as a reporter in synthetic biology, making it a valuable target for binder development. Teams working with GFP-tagged proteins could use such a binder for protein pull-down assays, surface immobilization, localization studies, and detection applications, providing a versatile alternative to conventional antibodies. Commercial anti-GFP nanobodies do this job well and have done so for years. They also cost several hundred dollars per aliquot, which is a trivial line item in a university core facility and an insurmountable one for a high school team or a team working without institutional backing. That gap is what we set out to close. A sequence published openly in the Registry costs a team only the price of synthesis and whatever expression they can already do, which for a binder of this size is within reach of any lab running basic recombinant protein work. The reagent itself is not novel; its accessibility is the contribution.

title: Contribution
section: How a Team Would Use It
text: The minibinder’s small size and predicted soluble expression in Escherichia coli make experimental production feasible using standard laboratory methods. The process involves synthesizing the coding sequence, incorporating a His-tag for purification, expressing the protein in E. coli , and isolating it through immobilized metal affinity chromatography (IMAC). Protein purity and molecular weight can then be assessed using SDS-PAGE. This workflow relies on techniques and equipment commonly available in molecular biology laboratories. GFP is particularly convenient for binding assays because its intrinsic fluorescence allows researchers to detect and monitor the protein without additional labeling. Teams can use fluorescence polarization or thermal shift assays to screen for potential binding interactions, while more advanced techniques, such as biolayer interferometry or surface plasmon resonance, can provide quantitative measurements of binding affinity. Including a commercial anti-GFP nanobody as a positive control also allows teams to compare their results against an established binder, helping distinguish weak binding interactions from unsuccessful designs.

title: Contribution
text: Future iGEM teams can build upon this work by experimentally validating the GFP minibinder, optimizing its expression and stability, and evaluating its performance in different applications. Once binding is confirmed, the design could be investigated for GFP-tagged protein purification, immobilization, localization, and detection. Teams can also adapt the documented computational workflow to develop minibinders against other proteins relevant to their projects.

title: Contribution
text: We developed VAPOR-X, a compact, automated vacuum-assisted drying system designed to remove moisture from biological materials at lower temperatures, reducing the risk of heat-induced degradation. Based on the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship, VAPOR-X uses a vacuum pump to lower the pressure inside a sealed chamber, allowing moisture to evaporate at temperatures below its normal atmospheric boiling point. A resistive heating pad provides controlled heating, while a thermistor and BME280 environmental sensor monitor temperature and chamber pressure. The system is controlled by a Raspberry Pi Pico W programmed in MicroPython, which uses a feedback loop to regulate heating and monitor vacuum conditions. By combining reduced-pressure drying with automated temperature control, VAPOR-X offers an accessible approach to preparing temperature-sensitive biological materials. To make VAPOR-X affordable, reproducible, and accessible to future iGEM teams, Lambert iGEM designed a custom printed circuit board (PCB), a 3D-printed enclosure, and an intuitive user interface featuring an OLED display and rotary encoder. title: Contribution
text: VAPOR-X contributes to the broader synthetic biology community by addressing the financial and technical barriers associated with conventional laboratory drying equipment. Commercial lyophilizers can cost thousands of dollars, making sample preservation and preparation difficult for underfunded laboratories, high school iGEM teams, and researchers in low-resource settings. By developing a vacuum-assisted drying system for under $100, we provide an affordable alternative for applications that do not require full freeze-drying capabilities. To ensure that future teams can reproduce and adapt our design, we have made our circuit schematics, hardware designs, and MicroPython code publicly accessible. These resources allow other iGEM teams to construct their own systems, modify operating parameters, and integrate vacuum-assisted drying into their experimental workflows. Through VAPOR-X, we hope to reduce the cost of laboratory equipment and expand access to experimental techniques across the synthetic biology community.

title: Contribution
text: To close the knowledge gap between wet-lab protocols and computational modeling for iGEM teams and students with limited modeling experience, we developed a seven-part video series, which is publicly available on YouTube (see Figure 1). Its framework takes viewers through a four-stage workflow showing how to use MATLAB SimBiology and export the resulting data into a readable graph. It explains how experimental workflows translate into computational models using individual protocols and wet-lab steps from Lambert’s internationally recognized LANCET project. We engineered an open-access template in MATLAB utilizing ordinary differential equations (ODEs) to give learners a starting point for exploring biochemical pathways and building their own models. This series helps teams predict system behavior and refine their designs, connecting modeling education to engineering. Overall, by making a modeling toolkit that others can learn from, adapt, and build upon, we are supporting broader participation in synthetic biology. Figure 1. Lambert iGEM YouTube Channel

title: Project Description
text: SWARM addresses a threat to one of agriculture’s most important pollinators. Honey bees visit crop flowers more often than any other single species, and many crops rely on them heavily [1]. In our home state of Georgia, beekeepers lost about 88,000 colonies between October 2025 and June 2026, translating to approximately 20% of the state’s colonies lost every three months [2]. Across the United States, beekeepers lost 39.9% of their managed colonies between April 2025 and April 2026 [3]. title: Project Description
text: SWARM began with four design requirements, drawn from the gaps in current treatments and from beekeepers’ needs: Treat DWV directly, since current guidance lists only mite treatments [14]. Reduce mites without the brood harm or wax residues of chemicals [14], [15]. Slow resistance, because mites already resist several miticides [6], [14]. Fit into hive routines as a practical, low-cost treatment. To meet them, SWARM pairs two treatments in one hive-top feeder: minibinders against DWV and dsRNA against Varroa. Bees would take in both treatments through the feeder’s sucrose solution. We designed the minibinders to act on the virus in the bee’s gut, and the dsRNA to reach the mite when it feeds on a treated bee, a route earlier researchers demonstrated [16]. title: Project Description
text: SWARM targets DWV with minibinders, small proteins designed on a computer to bind a specific target. We designed our minibinders against VP3, one of the proteins that form the virus’s outer shell, or capsid. Part of VP3 folds into a knob on the virus’s surface that may help the virus enter bee cells [17]. We designed the minibinders to inhibit viral replication by binding VP3 to block host cell binding. We compared minibinders with antibodies and with nanobodies, small antibody fragments from camels and llamas, and chose minibinders for their small size and heat tolerance (Table 2). Table 2. title: Project Description
text: SWARM targets the mite with RNA interference, a natural process in which cells use dsRNA to switch off target genes. When a mite cell takes in dsRNA that matches one of its genes, the cell destroys that gene’s messenger RNA (the working copy it uses to build a protein) to limit it from making that protein. We designed a multiplexed dsRNA that targets three Varroa salivary gland genes essential to mite survival. By designing novel siRNA sequences for Vd-CHIsal , Vd-CHIBIN , and VdAV422 , we are able to silence three genes compared to one in existing remedies [12]. Earlier work that silenced a single mite gene reduced mite populations by over 60%, so targeting three should not only boost efficacy but also limit the likelihood of resistance that mites are developing [16]. Our dsRNA approach is delivered through treated bees, the same route used to successfully silence mite genes in the past [16]. To address ecological concerns with reduced mite populations, we spoke to entomologist Jeff Pettis, who assured us it would be “completely fine to eliminate Varroa, as honeybees get no benefit at all from it” (see Integrated Human Practices ). Explore our RNAi design and experiments →

title: Project Description
text: SWARM reaches bees through a hive-top sucrose feeder. Our design dries the minibinders into a powder, intended to be shelf-stable, with a low-cost vacuum evaporator. The evaporator removes water at low temperature so heat does not unfold, or denature, the proteins. A three-chamber feeder holds the minibinder powder, a sucrose solution, and the dsRNA in separate compartments, so one unit delivers both treatments to the colony. Explore the hardware →

title: Engineering Success
text: Through our sponsorship with Adaptyv Bio, we experimentally screened our initial minibinder candidates against VP3. Despite favorable computational predictions, none of the tested minibinders demonstrated detectable binding under the assay conditions.

title: Engineering Success
text: The unsuccessful first batch revealed that favorable computational predictions did not necessarily translate into experimental binding. We identified two potential limitations in our design process: epitope selection, which determines where a minibinder interacts with VP3, and solubility, which can influence protein expression and experimental performance. These findings motivated us to refine our computational workflow by improving hotspot identification and incorporating additional sequence optimization before experimental testing.

title: Engineering Success
section: Iteration 1.2: Epitope Selection and Solubility Optimization

title: Engineering Success
text: Following the unsuccessful first batch, we revised our computational design approach to address potential limitations in epitope selection and solubility. To improve hotspot selection, we incorporated PRINCE, our software that combines computational structural analysis with literature-based evidence to identify promising binding regions (see Software ). This allowed us to target alternative epitopes on the VP3 P-domain rather than relying on the initial binding regions. We also incorporated SolubleMPNN, a protein sequence-design model that favors amino acid sequences with characteristics associated with soluble protein expression. By combining improved epitope selection with sequence optimization, we aimed to generate minibinders with more favorable predicted binding interactions and expression properties.

title: Engineering Success
text: Using PRINCE, we identified two new binding hotspots on the VP3 P-domain and generated a second batch of minibinders through our computational design pipelines. We evaluated the resulting designs using Protenix and Boltz-2, analyzing ipTM and iPAE to assess predicted interface confidence. We additionally used SolubleMPNN to redesign amino acid sequences with the goal of improving solubility while preserving their intended structures and binding interactions. These evaluations allowed us to prioritize promising candidates for a second round of experimental screening.

title: Engineering Success
text: We submitted our redesigned minibinder candidates to Adaptyv Bio for experimental binding analysis. Unlike the initial batch, the second batch produced one minibinder with experimentally detectable binding to VP3. This result demonstrated that our revised computational workflow successfully generated a candidate capable of binding the intended target.

title: Engineering Success
text: The second iteration demonstrated improved experimental outcomes following modifications to epitope selection and sequence optimization. While the initial batch produced no detectable binders, the revised workflow generated a successful VP3-binding minibinder. These findings highlighted the importance of evaluating not only predicted binding confidence but also the selection of appropriate epitopes and sequence properties relevant to protein expression. Although the improved outcome cannot be attributed to PRINCE or SolubleMPNN independently, the results support the effectiveness of our revised design workflow.

title: Engineering Success
text: The model follows nine quantities through each day. Adult bees are split into those carrying deformed wing virus and those without it, alongside a running total of the ones the virus has killed, and the mites are divided much the same way, into those alive and able to feed and the subset of those carrying virus they can pass on. They are the same equations run twice over the same weather, and the only thing that differs between the two runs is whether syrup is available.

title: Engineering Success
text: The first version kept every rate constant, with no seasons and no weather at all. A single bite rate carried the virus from mites to bees, infected bees were allowed to recover, and deaths from the virus came out of a term of their own. We drew the results as four separate figures, one population per figure, which seemed reasonable at the time.

title: Engineering Success
text: It ran, and the treated colony did better than the untreated one, which was encouraging for about a day. Underneath, three things were wrong. The bite rate was doing two jobs at once, setting both how often mites fed on bees and how often the virus actually moved between them, so there was no way to change one without dragging the other along with it. Recovery was worse, because we had infected adults returning to health at a steady rate and nothing in the deformed wing virus literature we were citing supports that. The virus death term had been written as the total death rate of an infected bee rather than the extra death the virus causes, so ordinary mortality and virus mortality were quietly counted against each other, which also forced an awkward constraint where the virus term had to come out larger than the baseline one for the arithmetic to behave. On top of all that, four populations on four separate axes meant nobody could put the treated and untreated colonies next to each other and see the difference. Original four RNAi Epidemiological models There is no seasonal cycle anywhere in these four, because there were no seasons yet, so the populations settle into flat equilibr

title: Engineering Success
text: The general lesson was to split anything doing two jobs, so transmission from mites to bees and pickup from bees to mites became two separate rates, which had the useful side effect of letting mites clear the virus again rather than carrying it for life. We also redefined the virus death rate as the extra daily mortality the virus adds, so an infected bee now dies at the ordinary rate plus that extra, infection always costs lifespan, and the constraint we had been working around disappeared on its own. Recovery stayed in the equations but is set to zero at every point in the year, which is deliberate. Leaving it visible as a stated assumption lets a reader see the decision and disagree with it, where deleting the term outright would have hidden the fact that a choice had been made at all.

title: Engineering Success
text: A colony with constant rates cannot answer the question we actually care about, because Varroa and deformed wing virus are both strongly seasonal and because overwintering is where colonies really die. So thirteen rates were each given four quarterly anchor values, read at the start of January, April, July and October and joined by a smooth curve that repeats from year to year. On top of that calendar we layered weather, standing in for the forage and conditions data we have no records for.

title: Engineering Success
text: The weather went in as four independent random series, one each for brood rearing, mites, bee survival and contact between the two, with each series carrying its own persistence, shock size and event scale. This pass also added most of the structure the model still has today: saturating gates so a small colony cannot rear brood or support mite reproduction efficiently, logistic mite growth against a capacity measured in mites per bee, a direct cost to adults from the mites feeding on them, crowding deaths once the colony outgrows its space, grooming, and a rule declaring a colony dead once it drops below a few hundred adults.

title: Engineering Success
text: Four problems came out of this version, and every one of them was found by reading the equations rather than by looking at the output. The weather was being held constant across each whole day, so multiplying a smooth seasonal curve by what amounted to a daily step function left the right-hand side of the differential equation jumping at every midnight, which meant the model was not differentiable in time and the solver had to be pinned to one-day steps to cope. Two of the saturating constants had their weather response backwards, which is easy to do and hard to spot, since a larger half-saturation constant makes brood care and mite reproduction worse rather than better, so giving them a positive weather sensitivity meant good weather was closing the brood gate instead of opening it. The gate on mite growth had been applied to the whole logistic expression rather than to births alone, so a colony that started to collapse also stopped culling its own mites and the load could run away completely. And four independent weather series, it turns out, cannot produce a bad summer at all, because nothing in them stops brood rearing from failing while mite conditions stay good. A fifth probl

title: Engineering Success
text: Three of those are really the same mistake in different clothing, and it is a mistake specific to models rather than to code, because an equation can be dimensionally correct, numerically stable and still completely wrong about the biology. A sign error on a saturating constant does not throw an error, it just quietly inverts the weather for the rest of the run, and a gate applied to the wrong half of a logistic term does not throw one either, it simply removes the brakes at precisely the moment a colony most needs them. Reading every functional form and asking what it was claiming about actual bees caught all four of these. Running the model and looking at the graphs caught none of them, which is the part we would want another team to take away from this.

title: Engineering Success
section: Iteration 3: Fixing the equations and re-sourcing the parameters

title: Engineering Success
text: Five changes, each aimed at one of the problems above, plus a pass back through every single parameter to check it against the source it was supposed to have come from.

title: Engineering Success
text: The weather driver is now interpolated between daily values, so every rate is continuous in time. The daily values themselves are unchanged and only the values in between are new. The two saturating constants take negative weather sensitivities, while the crowding threshold keeps a positive one, because more forage genuinely does let a colony hold more bees before crowding starts to cost it anything. Mite births are gated by colony size and density removal is not, since mites can only breed where there is capped brood but crowding kills them whether or not any brood exists. A single shared weather index now drives all four groups, each through its own loading, so a bad summer hits brood rearing, bee survival, mite conditions and virus spread together. Collapsing four series into one also removed about twenty numbers we had no source for. The brood term became an infested-cell calculation rather than an exponential decay. Cells entered per day comes from the invasion rate and the number of virus-carrying mites, cells capped per day is the potential emergence, and the emergence lost from an infested cell is a measured quantity. Same curve shape as before, but every piece of it can no

title: Engineering Success
text: The fifth change also settled something we had been getting wrong without realising it. Because coverage settles at a fixed ratio of uptake to loss, the potency, the uptake rate, the decay rate and the two parameters setting the shape of the dose-response all reach the data through a single product, which means they cannot be fitted separately at all. Raising the decay rate and raising the potency cancel each other almost exactly. Epidemiological models with colony collapse resolved. These are the same four panels as the set above, after the five fixes. The mite runaway is gone, and the untreated colony now fails for a reason the equations can defend rather than an arithmetic one.

title: Engineering Success
text: That leaves exactly one number in the treatment block that can be calibrated at all. The uptake rate, the dsRNA loss rate and the rate at which disabled mites die are all measurable in their own right, and the two shape parameters are held at published values, so the potency is the only thing left for data to pin down. The script solves for it against a mite reduction taken from the middle of the range reported for field trials of RNAi Varroa treatments. The calibration routine also carries a warning we wrote after being caught out by it. If the untreated colony collapses partway through, its mite count sits at zero for the rest of the run, so a reduction averaged across the whole horizon understates the treatment badly and can even come out negative. Every effect the model reports is now measured only over the days when both colonies are still alive.

title: Engineering Success
section: Iteration 4: Checking the result from outside

title: Engineering Success
text: Everything up to this point had come out of one script, one weather sequence and one team’s reading of its own work, which leaves three fairly obvious gaps. A result from a single weather is not really a result, the one-at-a-time sensitivity test only ever touched the six treatment parameters, and nobody had tried to re-derive the thing independently.

title: Engineering Success
text: So the model was rebuilt in Python, working from the equations rather than translating the MATLAB line by line, then checked against a GNU Octave run of the original. On top of that we ran a global analysis: a thousand Latin hypercube draws across every input in the model, with fresh weather for each draw, scored by partial rank correlation under a strict significance cut-off. Then six stress tests, each pushing one property at a time well past anything we would call nominal.

title: Engineering Success
text: The cross-check held comfortably. In fixed weather the two implementations agree to five decimal places, the spread across random weathers is statistically indistinguishable between them, halving the time step moves nothing worth reporting, and an older Python with older libraries produces identical output. Older version of the Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis for a particular parameter featured on the left, the newer version is featured on the right. The global analysis is where the result changed shape. Across a thousand draws both colonies survive in roughly four fifths of them, and in those the treatment removes around 96% of the feeding mites, with even the worst draw still above 84%. What was not obvious beforehand is that the two outcomes we care about turn out not to be controlled by the same things at all. Outcome What actually drives it Fewer feeding mites The potency of our dsRNA, by a wide margin, then the adult death rate and the emergence rate More adult bees The adult death rate, the mite growth rate and the natural mite death rate, in that order None of the six treatment parameters moves the bee gain by a significant amount.

title: Engineering Success
text: The honest reading of that table is that how many mites we remove is about the dsRNA, while how many more bees the colony ends up with is mostly about the colony’s own demography. We would rather say so plainly than let a reader assume our treatment sets the bee number directly, and there is a fairly mechanical reason behind it: a higher adult death rate produces a smaller untreated colony, a smaller colony was never going to carry many mites to begin with, and so the gap between treated and untreated narrows from the untreated side. The treated colony itself barely moves either way, because nearly all of its mite-days fall in the first year and after that there is almost nothing left to count. The stress tests suggest the headline is not fragile. A 90% reduction survives the uptake being cut to a quarter of what we plan to deliver, the dsRNA degrading several times faster than measured, and the potency being cut nearly in half, and it only really gives way when potency drops to a fifth of nominal, at which point the effect falls to roughly half. text: About minibinders The overall goal of this cycle was to develop and validate a system of expression by producing VP3 protein and de novo minibinders through plasmid cloning, cell-free expression, and Ni-NTA purification. About colony model

title: Engineering Success
text: One honeybee colony, simulated day by day for five years and run twice through the same weather: once left alone, and once fed sucrose syrup carrying dsRNA from the first day onward. Because the machine keeps fresh syrup available continuously, there is no feeding schedule to design and nothing to optimise about timing, which leaves a cleaner question underneath. Does the treatment actually hold Varroa and deformed wing virus down over the kind of timescale a beekeeper cares about, and how much should anyone trust the answer? Getting to something we were willing to defend took four passes, and each one broke a claim the pass before it had made. We have kept the broken versions here rather than quietly replacing them, partly because that is what an engineering cycle is supposed to look like, and partly because the failures turned out to be the most informative part of the whole exercise. title: Entrepreneurship
text: Figure 1. Varroa mites attached to a honey bee larva. The Varroa mite (see Figure 1), a parasite that spreads Deformed Wing Virus (DWV), is one of the greatest threats to honey bees. DWV weakens the colonies that beekeepers and farmers rely on for income and crop pollination, and it is spread by Varroa mites that feed on developing and adult honey bees. The virus can impair wing development, shorten bee lifespans, and weaken colonies. Together, Varroa and DWV can contribute to severe colony decline and even collapse (see Figure 2). Figure 2. Feedback loop of honey bee colony collapse. This critical issue is the focus of SWARM because beekeepers must manage Varroa throughout the year rather than through a single treatment. Mite populations can recover after treatment, and untreated populations can grow quickly within a colony. Beekeepers therefore monitor mite levels and apply treatments at different points in the season to keep populations below damaging levels.

title: Entrepreneurship
text: Lambert iGEM identified Varroa mites and Deformed Wing Virus (DWV) as a persistent challenge because beekeepers must manage both an aggressive parasite and the viruses it spreads. U.S. beekeepers lost an estimated 44.6% of managed honey bee colonies during the 2024–2024 season, the highest annual loss recorded by the national survey at that time (Giacobino et al., 2024). Current control methods also face growing limitations because repeated chemical use can select for resistant Varroa populations and reduce treatment effectiveness over time (Bertola & Mutinelli, 2024). At the same time, DWV can remain in infected bees without obvious physical symptoms, allowing the virus to spread before beekeepers recognize a problem (Gauthier et al., 2007). Varroa further intensifies this issue by acting as a major vector for DWV transmission between honey bees (Martin & Brettell, 2019). Together, treatment resistance, hidden viral spread, and continued colony loss create a clear gap in current Varroa and DWV management.

title: Entrepreneurship
text: Varroa mites are one of the leading causes of colony loss, creating recurring costs for beekeepers, and current solutions face resistance and inconsistent effectiveness. To address this gap, we created SWARM, a dual-sided platform combining a minibinder therapeutic targeting Deformed Wing Virus with RNAi designed to disrupt critical functions in Varroa salivary glands. By targeting both the mite itself and one of the major viruses it transmits, SWARM approaches the problem from two directions, aiming to reduce Varroa-related damage and improve long-term colony health. Since Varroa control requires seasonal treatment, the approach supports sustained demand and long-term profitability.

This creates a large downstream agricultural market in which maintaining healthier colonies can directly affect crop production, pollination availability, and beekeeper profitability. text: Despite its major impact on honey bee colony loss, Deformed Wing Virus still lacks a strong and direct antiviral solution. Current treatments mainly manage Varroa mites, but they do not directly stop DWV from entering bee cells, leaving beekeepers with an incomplete solution. With high market need and established beekeeper distribution channels, SWARM is positioned to become a scalable bee-health platform that protects colonies while supporting commercial agriculture.

To address this, Lambert iGEM developed a frugal vacuum dryer for under $85 USD using accessible components to perform a similar function as commercial units for a fraction of the cost, thereby making substance-drying accessible to all. title: Hardware
text: Vapor-X is built around the Clausius-Clapeyron relation: the evaporation temperature of a substance decreases as the air pressure of its environment decreases (Tatum, n.d.). Lambert iGEM’s hardware system uses a vacuum pump to lower the pressure inside an airtight mason jar, while a resistive heating pad heats a sample inside the mason jar. By heating substances in a vacuum chamber to temperatures lower than their normal boiling points at atmospheric pressure, Vapor-X can effectively dry substances while reducing the risk of degradation or melting at high temperatures. text: Because Vapor-X requires only an airtight jar, a vacuum pump, and a resistive heating pad, the system can be adapted for other applications involving heat-sensitive materials. Research laboratories and other iGEM teams without access to a lyophilizer could use Vapor-X to dehydrate proteins or enzymes for long-term storage. title: Inclusive Education
section: Week 1: Introduction to Synthetic Biology & Basic Lab Skills
text: In this lesson, students learn about what synthetic biology is and how they should conduct themselves in a lab setting. In addition, we teach them about our iGEM team and how we use synthetic biology.

title: Inclusive Education
section: Week 2: Understanding Units, Dimensional Analysis, and Lab Calculations
text: Week 2 is about understanding how to measure data. This week, we teach students about the units used for scientific research and how they are applied in experimentation.

title: Inclusive Education
text: In Week 3, we introduce students to DNA and how it functions within the body. Students learn about base pair interactions, mutations, and how the two can affect research.

title: Inclusive Education
text: During this week, we further explain DNA’s functions, this time expanding on the process of central dogma. Specifically, we cover transcription, translation, and other aspects of gene expression in biological systems.

title: Inclusive Education
section: Week 5: Introduction to Genetic Engineering Techniques
text: The Week 5 lesson is centered on genetic engineering. We first introduce students to bacterial transformation, transfection, and viral vectors, before concluding the lesson with an introduction to CRISPR and its uses in altering or suspending transcription.

title: Inclusive Education
text: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a key step in the gene editing process: without it, we would not have a large enough concentration of our target DNA sequences. In this week’s lesson, we explain how PCR functions and give students a brief overview of how gel electrophoresis is used to analyze and interpret results.

title: Inclusive Education
section: Week 7: Intro to Cloning and Synbio Tools
text: Week 7 focuses on the importance of cloning in synthetic biology, covering the steps taken in cloning and the different ways to purify cloned sequences. Much of this week’s lesson is about plasmids—we highlight plasmid design as a key step in the cloning process.

title: Inclusive Education
text: For anyone interested in working in synthetic biology in the future, one of the most important concerns to consider is ethics. This lesson asks students to truly think about whether or not certain experiments are okay to implement, using the five bioethics principles of autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, and responsibility as a guiding framework.

title: Inclusive Education
text: This lesson delves back into CRISPR, focusing this time on both its importance and its limitations. Students conduct a case study to better understand how CRISPR is used throughout synthetic biology today.

title: Inclusive Education
text: Week 10 introduces the concept of cell-free synthetic biology as an alternative to traditional in vivo systems. We emphasize that using cell-free systems can substantially reduce waiting time and allow scientists to better control their experiments, but caution students that there are limitations involved as well. We end the lesson with the thought that cell-free is a useful tool in synthetic biology, but there are still circumstances when traditional methods may be superior. It is up to the student to decide what works best for their particular experiment.

title: Inclusive Education
text: Week 11 is geared towards teaching students how to design experiments, then compile their data in a readable and replicable format. We highlight the importance of control groups as a baseline for experiment validity.

title: Inclusive Education
section: Week 12: Your Future in Synthetic Biology
text: We finalize the FFF semester by introducing potential career options within the field of synthetic biology to our students. We also include an in-depth lesson on SWARM as a real-world example of how the processes we’ve taught throughout the course can be implemented into a physical synthetic biology project. By the twelfth week, students are able to take the skills that they have learned throughout the course and apply them towards complex scientific concepts. Throughout the course, we challenge students with complex writing assignments that further expand their knowledge of synthetic biology and build critical thinking. At the end of the course, students are given the opportunity to express their thoughts on the class and give feedback on what we can improve. Many students told us that before taking this course, they had little understanding of synthetic biology and limited interest in science. title: Minibinder Overview
text: Initially, Lambert iGEM considered the use of nanobodies —antibody fragments derived from camelids — to bind the P-domain of VP3 of DWV. However, after meeting with nanobody specialist Aashish Manglik, a professor at the University of California, San Diego, our focus shifted to minibinders as they proposed greater potential wet-lab success. Minibinders also offered more promise with computational design tools and stability concerns (Bouchiba et al, 2022).

title: Minibinder Overview
text: Lambert iGEM designed de-novo minibinders to bind the P-domain of the VP3 protein of Deformed Wing Virus (DWV). The structure of DWV is an icosahedral capsid, a protein shell that protects the viral genome. Comprising the capsid are three structural proteins: VP1, VP2, and VP3. A polypeptide linker connects the VP3 protein to a P-domain that protrudes from the capsid. A Cyro-EM surface representation of DWV shows that portions of the VP1 and VP2 proteins are physically buried by the P-domain of the VP3 protein, rendering them ineffective targets in comparison to VP3 (Škubník et al., 2017). The surface representation of the P-domain shows an Asp-His-Ser catalytic triad that is thought to participate in protein-protein interactions and cell entry. The dependence on this residue maintains its sequence and confirmation across all variants of DWV (Škubník et al., 2017).

text: The hive is modeled as two 10-frame Langstroth deeps, which places a fixed comb ceiling on brood rearing. Within that space, the individual variation in age and infection status determines the colony level outcomes so the treatment would produce a different age structure or mite load. To ensure that every component carried an established background and that the model’s behavior could be attributed to known biology, we assembled it from published Varroa, DWV, and honey bee colony models. Four model families supply the backbone: Sumpter & Martin 2004 supplies the DWV block - the in-cell and phoretic transmission routes, seasonal brood death, and the epidemic threshold the model is later tested against. Khoury, Myerscough & Barron 2011 supplies colony demography: the saturating egg-laying term N/(w+N), the house-bee-to-forager recruitment rule R = α − σF/N, and the social-inhibition route to collapse. Betti, Wahl & Zamir 2014 supplies forager mortality on foraging days. BEEPOP/VarroaPop (DeGrandi-Hoffman et al.) and BEEHAVE (Becher et al. 2014) supply the weather-driven structure: egg laying as a function of temperature, photoperiod and colony size, and a foraging-day threshold on dai

text: Our colony model relies on structural assumptions that are adopted to keep the simulation computationally tractable at the scale of individual bees and mites over six years. We assume that mites attach to adult bees at random with respect to the task. Mites in the field attach to the nurse bees and this raises the probability that a mite reaches a brood cell. Mites enter the colony from surrounding apiaries at a constant daily rate in an invasion season. There is no horizontal bee to bee DWV transmission in the absence of a mite. Mites do not evolve resistance to the treatment and that the virus does not evolve over the years. Weather drives the colony through daily maximum temperature and that precipitation has no day to day persistence. A fixed comb ceiling of two 10 frame Langstroth deeps and a beekeeper who feeds on schedule when a feeding window is open. The queen is never lost, the colony never swarms, bees do not drift in or out, and no other treatments are applied. Treated and untreated colonies share the same starting conditions, parameters and weather, so any difference between them comes from the treatment. title: Minibinder Model
text: To predict how much minibinder reaches the site at which it must act, Lambert iGEM developed a compartmental model tracking protein from the feeder to the viral capsid. This pathway follows four main steps: Degradation: Protein dissolved in sucrose syrup degrades in the feeder across the refill interval. Ingestion: Foraging bees swallow the syrup, carrying protein into the crop. Transit: The crop empties into the midgut, where proteolysis and transit compete with absorption. Absorption: Intact protein crosses the midgut epithelium into the haemolymph, where it is cleared and where it binds free virions.

title: Minibinder Model
text: To simulate the progression of the delivery pathway, our team utilized a system of ODEs describing each compartment. Our model tracks amounts in nanomoles per bee rather than concentrations, which allows gut volume to be left unspecified and makes mass conservation an exact identity rather than a numerical tolerance. Because of this, oral bioavailability is produced as an output of the model rather than entered as an input. Binding to the viral capsid was represented as a reversible second-order association followed by irreversible clearance of the complex, using rate constants measured on our own construct. Binding is carried as a reversible second-order association with irreversible clearance of the complex, parameterised from our own BLI data.

title: Minibinder Model
text: We mapped out the full delivery pathway using the Law of Mass Action, which simulates basic collisions of reactants (see Fig. 1). The pathway begins with minibinder dissolved in sucrose solution at the feeder and ends in one of five terminal sinks: degraded in the syrup, digested in the gut, excreted, cleared from the haemolymph, or cleared as a neutralised complex.

title: Minibinder Model
text: Our compartmental ODE model assumes that all rate constants and parameters remain constant, disregarding external environmental factors. The model assumes that absorption across the midgut epithelium is linear, which is justified because the concentrations our schedule produces sit below the reported transport constant, where linear and saturable forms are not distinguishable. The model also assumes that protein reaching the hemolymph is intact and functional.

title: Minibinder Model
text: After developing a complete set of ODEs, we simulated all four compartments over four refill cycles at the adopted loading (see Fig. X). The bee reaches its periodic steady state within approximately one refill cycle, which indicates that protection does not accumulate with continued dosing. [Figure X - four state trajectory over four refill cycles] Our model predicts that of the protein placed in the feeder, 61.9% survives a 24 hour refill in warm syrup, and 0.300% of what is swallowed reaches the hemolymph as intact functional protein. The 15 µL of hemolymph it enters clears it with a half-life of 4.5 hours. The product of these losses determines the required dose (see Table X). [insert table x] The periodic cycle closing to 6.21 × 10⁻²² indicates that the periodic steady state is exact rather than approximate. The agreement between the emergent and closed-form values of oral bioavailability confirms that the compartmental structure is internally consistent.

title: Minibinder Model
text: Our dose criterion evaluates a single circulating concentration, which requires the concentration profile between refills to remain flat. To achieve this, Lambert iGEM modeled the feeder volume and refill interval together, sizing the feeder so that drain time equals the refill interval exactly.

title: Minibinder Model
text: A feeder that empties before the next refill leaves the colony without protein for part of every cycle, producing a deep trough and requiring a much higher peak concentration to compensate. Rather than treat this as a biological constraint, our team treated feeder volume as a design variable and solved for the volume at which drain time matches the refill interval. The colony draw rate was modeled at the colony level from standard practice guidance for a strong colony, and was deliberately not decomposed into a per-bee rate.

title: Minibinder Model
text: Our refill schedule model assumes that the residual batch is replaced rather than topped up at each refill, which is the conservative convention because it discards whatever active protein remains. The model also assumes that syrup is drawn uniformly by the colony at the modeled rate throughout the interval.

title: Minibinder Model
text: We simulated haemolymph binder concentration across four refill cycles beginning from an empty bee (see Fig. X). The peak-to-trough ratio is 1.128, indicating that the remaining ripple is the refill cycle itself rather than a swing the criterion must average over. Concentration rises while the bee drinks and falls as protein clears with a 4.5 hour half-life, and each cycle returns to the same value. [Figure X] The adopted schedule parameters and their basis are listed below (see Table 9). [Table X] The 24 hour interval was taken from the only published experiment that fed an anti-DWV protein to bees in syrup, which replaced feed daily. The feeder volume was not measured but chosen, so that the feeder drains in exactly one interval and the flat profile our criterion requires is maintained.

title: Minibinder Model
text: The circulating concentration is the quantity the bee experiences, but the mass of powder is the quantity a beekeeper must weigh out. To convert between them, our team inverted the delivery model to obtain the syrup concentration that holds the required haemolymph level, then multiplied by feeder volume and refill count to obtain the hive-scale figure.

title: Minibinder Model
text: Because the delivery cascade is linear, the inversion admits a closed form, so our team derived one rather than solving numerically. The closed form is checked against an independent root-find on each model run. If that check were to fail, the delivery model would no longer be linear and every mass figure would be invalid. Molecular weight and reconstitution recovery enter the inversion as exact linear multipliers, which allows the mass figure to be rescaled without re-running the model if the construct changes.

title: Minibinder Model
text: Our inversion model assumes that reconstitution recovery remains constant across batches, and that syrup is shared uniformly across the colony at the modeled draw rate.

title: Minibinder Model
text: We traced the mass of protein through each stage from weighed powder to absorbed protein (see Fig. X). The overall reduction across the cascade is a factor of 634, and each contributing multiplier is accounted for separately (see Table X). [Figure X] [Table x] Inverting the delivery model at the required haemolymph level gives a syrup concentration of 15.82 mg/mL, equivalent to 1.582% w/v, which corresponds to 82.4 g of powder per hive per week (see Table 11). At this concentration the formulation is an ordinary sucrose syrup, which is the condition our hardware was designed to handle. [Table X]

title: Minibinder Model
text: The quantity our platform must improve is not the amount of virus destroyed, but the frequency with which a mite bite fails to start an infection. Field measurements report that 39.8% of mites induce an overt infection in an untreated bee. To predict how circulating minibinder changes that frequency, Lambert iGEM developed a dose-response model relating syrup concentration to the probability that a single bite establishes an infection.

title: Minibinder Model
text: Our team derived the establishment probability in closed form from the number of particles delivered per bite. A mite delivers a countable number of effective genome equivalents, each of which either starts a productive infection or is neutralised before it can. Circulating binder changes the probability that any individual particle escapes neutralization, and the probability of establishment per bite follows by compounding that escape probability across the delivered inoculum. Sweeping syrup concentration across the deliverable range then produces the full dose-response relationship.

title: Minibinder Model
text: Our dose-response model assumes that the criterion applies per encounter rather than per season, as the model carries no mite encounter rate. The model also assumes that the reported field establishment probability combines the likelihood that a mite was infectious at all with the likelihood that an infection established, so the binder is credited in part for mites carrying no infectious virus.

title: Minibinder Model
text: We simulated the reduction in new infections across syrup concentrations spanning the deliverable range (see Fig. 5). The adopted concentration of 15.82 mg/mL produces a 74.9% reduction in new infections, with a half-maximal concentration of 5.34 mg/mL and a ceiling of 87.5%. [FIGURE 5 — PLACEHOLDER: prevention dose-response curve] Figure X The syrup concentration and weekly hive mass required for each target reduction are listed below (see Table X). Above a reduction of 87.5% the limiting constraint ceases to be concentration and becomes the fraction of virus the binder can physically reach, so the curve approaches a vertical asymptote rather than approaching complete prevention. Our team therefore specified a target within the attainable range rather than quoting a reduction the chemistry cannot deliver.

title: Minibinder Model
text: Our deterministic models treat virus as a continuous concentration, but a mite does not deliver a concentration. It delivers a countable handful of infectious particles, and each one either starts a productive infection or is cleared beforehand. At these particle numbers the outcome is governed by chance, so an average concentration is not an appropriate description. To address this, Lambert iGEM developed a stochastic model of establishment using the Gillespie algorithm.

title: Minibinder Model
text: The Gillespie algorithm simulates the exact sequence of discrete events in the system, drawing the waiting time to each event from its own rate: one particle infects a cell, another is cleared, an infected cell bursts. Running the simulation many times produces the probability that an infection establishes rather than an average viral load. Our team then compared that simulated probability against the closed-form branching calculation. Because the two are derived by completely different methods, agreement between them indicates that the establishment threshold is a real property of the system rather than an artefact of either approach.

title: Minibinder Model
text: Our stochastic model assumes that each delivered particle acts independently of the others, and that the branching process is evaluated at the initial availability of target cells.

title: Minibinder Model
text: We simulated establishment probability across a grid of delivered particle counts and compared the result against the closed-form branching probability (see Fig. 6). The two methods agree to within 3.46 standard errors, and the branching identity closes to 4.46 × 10⁻¹⁶. [Figure X] These results indicate that the deterministic threshold and the stochastic threshold describe the same property of the system, reached by two independent derivations.

title: Minibinder Model
text: To determine which parameters control the required loading and how much the answer could move given what remains unmeasured, Lambert iGEM performed two complementary sensitivity analyses and one joint uncertainty propagation. Elasticity analysis measures how far the answer moves per unit change in a single parameter. Sobol analysis measures how much of the total variance in the answer each parameter is responsible for when all parameters vary together, including through their interactions.

title: Minibinder Model
text: The elasticities were derived analytically from the closed form of the delivery chain rather than estimated from samples, which is why several values fall at exactly plus or minus one. The Sobol indices were computed from 24,576 model evaluations with every declared parameter bracket swept simultaneously. A third analysis propagated all declared brackets jointly across 3,000 draws to produce a distribution of required loading.

title: Minibinder Model
text: Our sensitivity analyses assume that Sobol indices are conditional on the ranges sampled, so a parameter may score low either because it has little effect or because its range is already narrow. The joint uncertainty band assumes the declared brackets contain the true values, and is a prior-predictive distribution over those ranges rather than a posterior, because no pharmacokinetic measurement in bees is available to condition on.

title: Minibinder Model
text: Perturbing each of the 114 scalars on the live model showed that 17 can move the required loading and 97 cannot. The elasticity of each is listed below (see Table 14), where an elasticity of plus one indicates that the required dose is exactly proportional to that parameter. [Table X] The total-order Sobol indices are listed below (see Table 15). First-order indices account for 96.7% of the total variance, indicating that the response is close to additive and that interactions between parameters carry only a small remainder. [Table X] The two tables must be interpreted together. The dissociation constant scores near zero in the Sobol analysis but almost exactly plus one in the elasticity analysis. Sobol indices attribute variance, so a parameter whose range is already narrow contributes little variance regardless of how strong its effect is. The sampled range of the dissociation constant spans roughly 1.2 times, while the haemolymph half-life spans three times. The elasticity analysis is therefore the correct table for reading effect size. Propagating every declared bracket simultaneously across 3,000 draws gives a 5th to 95th percentile span of 14.0 times, from 0.462% to 6.45% w/v

text: To establish how much an improvement in binding affinity would reduce the required material, Lambert iGEM modeled the relationship between the dissociation constant of the construct and the syrup concentration needed to meet the criterion.

title: Minibinder Model
text: Our team derived the relationship from the closed form of the requirement rather than fitting it, and the required dose was found to be exactly linear in the dissociation constant. This linearity is asserted in our test suite on each model run. We then mapped the resulting relationship against the field and laboratory concentrations of a registered dsRNA product for Varroa control, so that an affinity target could be expressed in terms of a product already in use.

text: Our affinity model assumes that an improvement in affinity arrives without changing molecular weight or reconstitution recovery, both of which enter the required loading as independent linear multipliers.

title: RNAi Model
text: The RNAi ODE model assumes rate constants as continuous, as Sf9 cultures are held at a constant 27 °C without external environmental factors that could alter them. Therefore, the model is able to isolate the silencing process to simulate knockdown of the Renilla reporter. The model also assumes that the initial quantities of siRNA, Argonaute-2, Dicer-2, and the psiCHECK-2 reporter are known, and that the cytoplasm behaves as a single well-mixed compartment. Additionally, the model assumes that synthetic 21-mer siRNA duplexes bypass Dicer-2 processing, that all three target sites sit within a single Renilla transcript, and that RISC cleaves that transcript at a constant rate regardless of which siRNA is loaded.

text: We evaluated RNAi knockdown in Sf9 cells using a modified psiCHECK-2 reporter containing each target sequence downstream of Renilla luciferase. We replaced the SV40 promoter driving Renilla with HSV-TK to support reporter expression in insect cells (Deng et al., 2022). title: RNAi Overview
text: Varroa destructor relies on salivary enzymes to feed on honeybees, digesting host tissue externally before ingesting it (Ramsey et al., 2019). As a result, the mite’s saliva carries Deformed Wing Virus (DWV): 9 DWV proteins have been identified in the mite’s salivary secretome (Zhang & Han, 2019). Therefore, RNAi knockdown of a salivary enzyme gene can disrupt feeding and viral transmission while reducing mite survival by 40–50% (Becchimanzi et al., 2024). To select our target genes, we developed a set of criteria that ensure our RNAi system is effective and safe: Targets encode for genes that are critical to the feeding function and survival of V. destructor Sequence is consistent across mite species with low mutation rate Minimal side effects to the health of the bee colony when our targets are silenced Sequence is unique to V. destructor We accordingly applied these criteria to the genome of V. destructor, and considered several targets, eventually finalizing on the genes Vd-CHIsal, Peritrophin-A, and Vdav422 (see Table 3). title: Software Writeups
text: PRINCE combines computational hotspot analysis with literature to identify biologically relevant epitopes for de novo minibinder design.

title: Software Writeups
text: Inspired by established epitope prediction tools such as BepiPred and DiscoTope, PRINCE evaluates: Solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) Hydrophobic residue distributions Local structural properties These properties identify accessible and favorable binding regions based on their predicted suitability for protein binding.

title: Software Writeups
text: PRINCE’s key innovation is incorporating existing experimental literature into epitope prediction. Many protein targets have published studies identifying functional regions, experimentally validated binding sites, or unsuccessful binding attempts. To leverage this information, we trained a large language model (LLM) to analyze relevant literature, extract biological evidence, and evaluate its implications for candidate epitopes. PRINCE then weighs this literature-derived evidence alongside structural scores to produce an informed epitope ranking supported by experimental knowledge alongside protein design pipelines.

title: Software Writeups
text: Using PRINCE, we conducted a second DWV minibinder campaign targeting two newly identified hotspots and were able to generate the first successful binder for DWV . We also applied PRINCE to GFP. Experimental results are pending.

title: Software Writeups
text: We benchmarked PRINCE using the Structural Antibody Database (SAbDab), comprising 8,241 antibody-antigen interfaces divided into cluster-disjoint training, validation, and testing sets. In our current evaluation, PRINCE successfully identified 83% of known epitopes , demonstrating its potential to recover experimentally characterized binding regions.

title: Software Writeups
text: Web Application: An accessible interface for epitope analysis and hotspot prediction without programming experience. Command-Line Interface (CLI): Enables automated analysis and integration into existing protein design pipelines. Open-Source Repository: Our iGEM GitLab contains the complete codebase, documentation, and protein datasets used in development and validation, supporting reproducibility and further improvement.

title: Software Writeups
text: PRINCE extends beyond DWV by providing literature-informed hotspot selection for diverse protein targets. Future development will focus on expanding validation across protein families, improving literature-based predictions, and integrating more directly with existing binder design tools.
